title: Your FriXion edits: which version survives 60°C? | Brand Stories
description:
What does a pen that writes, erases and writes again actually leave on paper? Follow one FriXion correction through color-change materials with memory, smaller microcapsules and mass production, and into a user's draft today. Color returning in the cold—and the limits of full recovery—help determine which pen belongs on that page. Historical accounts are attributed to the maker and developers. Anonymous concept illustrations do not depict documented contemporary scenes or a cutaway of the retail ink formula.

c15r1h01.text: You have just corrected a page of notes. If the paper reaches 60°C, which version will remain?

c15r1h02.text: A PILOT sales representative later recalled a trial sale at a Japanese stationery specialty shop: customers wrote with the pen themselves, then rubbed the marks with its eraser.

c15r1h03.text: To me, that action is harder to explain than an advertisement: how does one end deal with what the nib has just left behind?

c15r1h04.text: Behind it is also a batch of capsules waiting to leave a small beaker.

c15h04b1.text: And temperature may have another say in what happens to the finished page.

c15r1h05.text: Follow a single FriXion correction through more than 30 years of color-change research to see how it reached your hand.

c15r1h06.text: One pen writes, erases and writes again. What does it leave on paper, and what does it leave up to temperature?

c15r1a01.text: Imagine correcting a draft. Draw a line with this pen first; before you actually erase it, your hand needs to pause.

c15r1a02.text: The current instructions say to wait for the ink to dry before touching the paper with the attached special eraser.

c15a02b1.text: How was the material that touches the paper chosen?

c15a02c1.text: In a sidebar on eraser materials, the maker says it needs elasticity and wear resistance; the eraser itself must withstand repeated use.

c15r1a03.text: If you only see the rubbing action, it is easy to think of this as another rubber eraser. How does it make the color disappear?

c15r1a04.text: Rubbing with the special eraser generates heat, making the ink on the paper colorless. This decoloring produces no erasing debris.

c15r1a05.text: The temperature in our opening question is the decoloring threshold listed in the current ink explanation.

c15r1a07.text: So what can happen next in that same spot?

c15r1a08.text: You turn the pen back around and write where the color disappeared, putting new content in the same place.

c15r1a09.text: I like the convenience: you do not have to move the correction to the side of the page or draw another line to make room for the new content.

c15r1a10.text: But if the color is merely hidden, why does the old line not immediately reappear when you let go?

c15r1a11.text: To answer that, we need to zoom into the marks. Tiny microcapsules serve as the color material.

c15r1a12.text: Each capsule contains a component that determines the color, one that makes it develop, and material that adjusts the color-change temperature.

c15r1a13.text: Those three jobs fit into one tiny space. Can a dye that determines black, red and other colors develop color on its own?

c15r1a14.text: Developer Senga explains that the dye shows black, red and other colors only when it combines with a color developer.

c15r1a15.text: The temperature-adjusting agent acts on that combination, determining the temperature at which the color changes state.

c15r1a18.text: To keep that old line corrected, what difficulty did developers first face with the adjusting agent?

c15r1b06.text: Looking back at the early material, the maker says its color changed slowly as it warmed and returned when left alone; even the transition was not sharply defined.

c15r1b07.text: The team focused on the adjusting agent and first made a high-sensitivity type: its color changed quickly at a certain temperature.

c15r1b08.text: This type also regained color quickly when cooled below a point near that temperature. The change was sharper, but a correction still would not stay put.

c15r1b09.text: To me, this is the key: to keep your correction from immediately reversing after you stop, could those two temperatures be separated?

c15r1b10.text: Development then turned to a memory type: after heat changed its color, it would regain color only when cooled to another, lower preset temperature.

c15r1b12.text: How far apart were the color-change and color-return points in the early memory type?

c15r1b13.text: The company records that in 1988 it could retain its color state across a gap of about 20 degrees. To widen that gap, how would they find the adjusting agent?

c15r1b14.text: The gap depended on the choice of adjusting agent. Senga recalls that they started with substances that already existed.

c15r1b15.text: Later, the team made more than 1,000 original compounds themselves, seeking agents that would set the desired color-change temperatures.

c15r1b16.text: But getting those materials to the end you write with required more than a wider temperature range. They still had to get through the nib.

c15r1b17.text: How large were those little color-changing capsules at the time?

c15r1c01.text: According to the maker's retrospective, the early capsules were about 10 to 15 micrometers in diameter, shrinking to five to 10 micrometers at the memory-type stage.

c15r1c02.text: Yet those capsules were still too large for ink to flow smoothly through the tiny gaps in a ballpoint tip.

c15r1c04.text: I had not expected smaller capsules to have thinner, more fragile shells. Beyond thinness, what challenge would the ink bring?

c15r1c06.text: Once mixed into ink, the capsules also encountered solvents and additives. Senga says many were poorly compatible with the capsules.

c15r1c07.text: So the shell had to be strong and withstand those ingredients. The team also studied the encapsulation methods and conditions.

c15r1c08.text: In the early 2000s, capsules shrank to about two to three micrometers, making them usable in pen ink. Which pen came first?

c15r1c09.text: After overcoming the nib problem, a decorating pen called ILLUSION appeared in 2002.

c15r1c10.text: It wrote in black; rubbing with the special eraser on the cap changed the black into another color.

c15r1c11.text: But if you wanted to correct a misspelled word, changing its color still left the old writing in the same place.

c15r1c12.text: After seeing this pen, a marketing employee at the European subsidiary asked the development lead: could it go from colored to transparent?

c15r1c14.text: The company explains this through pen use in France: certain inks could be treated with an ink eradicator, but could the original pen then write there again?

c15r1c15.text: Where the eradicator had soaked in, the original pen could not rewrite. You needed another, dedicated pen.

c15r1c18.text: Development also had to address everyday temperature changes. The retrospective records a range from zero to 40°C; outside it, the color state could change.

c15r1c19.text: A later adjusting agent extended that historical development range to minus 20 to 65°C, a gap of 85 degrees.

c15r1c17.text: The material worked in a small beaker. To make it a product, what had to stay consistent in mass production?

c15r1d01.text: The maker recalls deciding on commercialization in 2004. The project had to produce ink at the factory in large quantities, with the same quality as in the beaker.

c15r1d02.text: Looking just at the capsule step, how much had to be produced reliably?

c15r1d03.text: The capsules waiting to leave the beaker in our opening amount to 500 kilograms in Senga's recollection of mass production.

c15r1d04.text: This required technology for stable capsule production. What problems arose on scaling up that a small beaker did not have?

c15r1d05.text: One was separation or deterioration after the capsules were made into ink. Being able to make capsules did not finish the job.

c15r1d06.text: Ink developers had to work with product design, production equipment and planning to deal with these problems together.

c15r1d07.text: To me, that is harder than finding a material that loses color. Other people do not have that successful beaker—how can they buy it?

c15r1d08.text: The maker describes this collaboration across departments as the process of overcoming mass-production obstacles. In 2006, FriXion launched first in Europe.

c15r1d09.text: Before bringing the product to Japan, the sales team put pens in stationery-shop customers' hands. What happened after they tried them?

c15r1d10.text: The trial sale with writing and erasing in our opening centered on hands-on experience. Sales representative Suzuki recalls that customers saw the color disappear, and some then bought the pen.

c15r1d12.text: In March 2007, the pen launched in Japan. There was now a tool you could buy directly for corrections on paper.

c15r1d14.text: That temperature gap was widened to keep corrections in place. When heat or cold reaches the other end, how else might it change this page?

c15r1e01.text: First, return the draft to everyday surroundings. Current instructions say direct sunlight, heat-generating equipment or a nearby cup of hot water can make the writing faint or colorless.

c15r1e02.text: If the page we worried about at the start really does lose color from heat, the maker offers another answer: cooling can start bringing the color back.

c15r1e03.text: The explanation states a limit first: definite color recovery is not guaranteed. So where does it put the start of recoloring?

c15r1e04.text: It says recoloring begins below minus 10°C, with the characteristic of full recoloring at around minus 20°C.

c15r1e06.text: What I want to know is this: where you rewrote, will the cold select the latest version for you?

c15r1e07.text: The maker explicitly says overlapping writing regains color together. Old marks erased earlier may appear among the new content.

c15r1e08.text: For writing rubbed out by friction, the instructions directly say its color cannot return completely. Cooling the paper is no undo button.

c15r1e09.text: If extreme heat or intense direct ultraviolet light has damaged the ink's components, the maker also says the color cannot be restored.

c15r1e10.text: Does that mean all writing of this kind is destined to disappear quickly?

c15r1e11.text: The maker's answer on long-term storage does not say that. Avoiding the high temperatures mentioned earlier allows preservation comparable to other dye-based gel inks.

c15r1e12.text: It also retains the condition that ultraviolet light gradually fades the writing, without guaranteeing a lifespan for every sheet.

c15r1e13.text: So if what you must hand over is a certificate or an address where writing must not disappear, change pens. The maker prohibits these uses.

c15e13b1.text: Even if it stays a draft, is the paper in your hand suited to this repeated rubbing?

c15e13c1.text: The maker lists rough paper and Japanese washi as surfaces that may be damaged by friction; coated paper may also be harder to write on.

c15r1e15.text: My answer to our opening question is this: the pen leaves the color's state up to temperature. It leaves you a page you can edit, but whose purpose you must choose.

c15r1ct1.text: Tell us in the comments which page you most often correct with this kind of pen: a schedule, a draft or your own notes.

c15r1ct2.text: To see how familiar objects put choices about materials into your hands, subscribe to Brand Stories.
